steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the Algorithm section of an encyclopedia article on adaptive heap sort: how it differs from standard heap sort, how it uses a Cartesian tree, and a short pseudo-code implementation.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- What adaptive heap sort is, compared with standard heap sort
- The algorithm using a Cartesian tree
- Pseudo-code

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Adaptive heap sort vs heap sort
  - variant of heap sort; seeks (asymptotic) optimality w.r.t. lower bound from the measure of presortedness, uses existing order in data
  - heap sort: data X = \langle x_1, x_2, x_3, \dots ,x_n \rangle , put all n elements in heap, extract max (or min) n times
  - each extraction logarithmic in heap size -> total \color{Blue} O(n \log n)
  - adaptive: only possible maximums (max-candidates) go into heap -> fewer runs to locate max (or min)
- Algorithm
  - build Cartesian tree from input in O(n): binary tree, each node greater (or smaller) than its children
  - root of Cartesian tree inserted into empty binary heap
  - repeat: extract max from heap, retrieve max in Cartesian tree, add its left and right children (themselves Cartesian trees) to heap
  - nearly sorted input -> very unbalanced Cartesian trees, few nodes with both children -> heap stays small -> faster than O(n\log n)
- Pseudo-code
  - input: array of n elements
  - construct Cartesian tree l(x); insert root into heap
  - loop 1..n: ExtractMax; if element has children in l(x), retrieve them and insert into heap

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Adaptive heap sort is a variant of heap sort. It tries to be optimal (asymptotically optimal) with respect to the lower bound that is derived with the measure of presortedness, and it does this by taking advantage of the order that already exists in the data. In heap sort, for a data X = \langle x_1, x_2, x_3, \dots ,x_n \rangle , all n elements are put into the heap and then the maximum (or minimum) is extracted n times. Each max-extraction takes time that is logarithmic in the size of the heap, so the total running time of standard heap sort is \color{Blue} O(n \log n) . In adaptive heap sort, instead of putting all of the elements into the heap, only the possible maximums of the data (max-candidates) are put into the heap, so that fewer runs are needed each time we try to find the maximum (or minimum).

- algorithm
  - build Cartesian tree from input in O(n): binary tree, each node greater (or smaller) than its children; root into empty binary heap
  - repeat: extract max from heap, retrieve max in Cartesian tree, add its left and right children (Cartesian trees) to heap
  - nearly sorted input -> unbalanced trees, few nodes with both children, heap stays small -> faster than O(n\log n)
- pseudo-code
  - input array of n elements; construct Cartesian tree l(x); insert root into heap
  - for i = from 1 to n: ExtractMax; if children in l(x), retrieve and insert into heap

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Adaptive heap sort is a variant of heap sort. It tries to be optimal (asymptotically optimal) with respect to the lower bound that is derived with the measure of presortedness, and it does this by taking advantage of the order that already exists in the data. In heap sort, for a data X = \langle x_1, x_2, x_3, \dots ,x_n \rangle , all n elements are put into the heap and then the maximum (or minimum) is extracted n times. Each max-extraction takes time that is logarithmic in the size of the heap, so the total running time of standard heap sort is \color{Blue} O(n \log n) . In adaptive heap sort, instead of putting all of the elements into the heap, only the possible maximums of the data (max-candidates) are put into the heap, so that fewer runs are needed each time we try to find the maximum (or minimum).

First a Cartesian tree is built from the input in O(n) time. This is done by putting the data into a binary tree and making each node in the tree greater (or smaller) than all of its children nodes. The root of the Cartesian tree is then inserted into an empty binary heap. After that the algorithm repeatedly extracts the maximum from the binary heap, retrieves the maximum in the Cartesian tree, and adds its left and right children (if there are any) to the binary heap, and these children are themselves Cartesian trees. When the input is already nearly sorted, the Cartesian trees will be very unbalanced and few nodes will have left and right children. This means the binary heap stays small, and the algorithm can sort more quickly than O(n\log n) for inputs that are already nearly sorted.

Here is an implementation in pseudo-code:

Input: an array of n elements that need to be sorted

Construct the Cartesian tree l(x)

Insert the root of l(x) into a heap

for i = from 1 to n

Perform ExtractMax on the heap

if the max element extracted has any children in l(x)

retrieve the children in l(x)

insert the children element into the heap

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Adaptive heap sort is a variant of heap sort that seeks optimality (asymptotically optimal) with respect to the lower bound derived with the measure of presortedness, by taking advantage of the existing order in the data. In heap sort, for a data X = \langle x_1, x_2, x_3, \dots ,x_n \rangle , we put all n elements into the heap and then keep extracting the maximum (or minimum) n times. Since each max-extraction takes time logarithmic in the size of the heap, the total running time of standard heap sort is \color{Blue} O(n \log n) .[1] For adaptive heap sort, instead of putting all the elements into the heap, only the possible maximums of the data (max-candidates) are put into the heap, so that fewer runs are required each time we try to locate the maximum (or minimum).

First, a Cartesian tree is built from the input in O(n) time by putting the data into a binary tree and making each node in the tree greater (or smaller) than all its children nodes, and the root of the Cartesian tree is inserted into an empty binary heap. Then the algorithm repeatedly extracts the maximum from the binary heap, retrieves the maximum in the Cartesian tree, and adds its left and right children (if any), which are themselves Cartesian trees, to the binary heap. If the input is already nearly sorted, the Cartesian trees will be very unbalanced, with few nodes having left and right children, so the binary heap remains small and the algorithm can sort more quickly than O(n\log n) for inputs that are already nearly sorted.[2]

Below is an implementation in pseudo-code:[3]

Input: an array of n elements that need to be sorted

Construct the Cartesian tree l(x)

Insert the root of l(x) into a heap

for i = from 1 to n

Perform ExtractMax on the heap

if the max element extracted has any children in l(x)

retrieve the children in l(x)

insert the children element into the heap
